title: The chip-rule text is public. The start date is still blank.
friendlyTitle: The chip rule is public. The start date is still blank.
summary: A Commerce Department interim-rule text, reported by TechCrunch on 16 November, would require licenses to send advanced AI chips and servers to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant compute to companies based in Country Group D:5 or Macau. It would also require a license for advanced chips going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil, with an exception for US-headquartered companies if reporting conditions are met. The public PDF still has blank Federal Register dates.
friendlySummary: A US Commerce Department draft, reported by TechCrunch on 16 November, would make companies get a license before sending advanced AI chips to some data centers abroad. The rule would cover centers that rent a lot of computing power to firms in a restricted country group, or in Macau. It would also cover chips sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil, with an exception for US parent companies that file reports. The public copy still has no start date.
whyItMatters: This is the text of a control, not a notice that is already in force. If you rent training compute outside the United States, the practical question is whether the data center would have to know who ultimately uses it. Retail and social recommender systems are carved out in the text.
friendlyWhyItMatters: This is a draft, not a rule that is already in force. If you rent training computers outside the United States, the useful question is whether the data center must know who ends up using them. The text leaves out ordinary recommendation systems, such as shop or social-media ranking.
